Chapter 1
Introduction and Scope
1.1 Welcome
Welcome to the Biology Graduate Programs at Delaware State University. The Department
of Biological Sciences advances research, training, and professional development across three
graduate pathways:
• MS in Biological Sciences
• MS in Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience
• PhD in Neuroscience
This handbook sets clear expectations for admission, coursework, research training, milestones,
professional conduct, and degree completion. It is written to the standards expected of
top research universities while reflecting DSU’s identity and mission as an HBCU with a
student-centered culture of excellence and inclusion.
1.2 What this handbook is and is not
This handbook provides department- and program-level requirements, procedures, and
expectations. University and Graduate School policies are authoritative and take precedence
over this handbook. Where a conflict exists, School of Graduate, Adult, and Extended Studies
(SGAES) and University policies govern. Students are responsible for staying current with
University deadlines and rules published by SGAES.
1.3 Audience and applicability
The handbook applies to all MS and PhD students in the Department of Biological Sciences,
their advisors, and members of graduate committees. It also informs staff and administrators
who support graduate education in the College of Agriculture, Science & Technology (CAST).
The policies herein apply from the date of matriculation until the conferral of the degree,
including any sustaining registration periods.
6
1.4 Programs at a glance
MS programs
The MS in Biological Sciences and the MS in Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience are
research-intensive degrees designed for completion in approximately two years of full-time
study, including summers. Each requires a total of 30 credits, typically 27 credits of graduate
coursework plus 3 credits of thesis research. Each student completes a mentored thesis, a
public seminar, and a thesis defense.
PhD in Neuroscience
The PhD requires a minimum of 60 credits (coursework plus dissertation research), qualifying
examinations, advancement to candidacy, an original dissertation, and a public defense.
Professional development and, where applicable, teaching training are integrated into the
program.
1.5 R1 standards; HBCU identity
DSU is pursuing an R1 research profile. Accordingly, this handbook emphasizes rigorous
research training, scholarship of publishable quality, structured milestones with clear timelines,
and a culture of high expectations. Equally, as an HBCU, the Department affirms an
inclusive, supportive environment that develops scholars prepared to lead in academia,
industry, government, and society.
1.6 Governance and decision-making
Department-level graduate policies are overseen by the Graduate Program Committee (GPC)
in consultation with research advisors and program directors. The Department Chair has
ultimate departmental authority for graduate matters within University policy. Advisors
direct day-to-day research training, with committees providing independent oversight and
guidance. Students are expected to maintain proactive communication with their advisors
and committees.
1.7 Using this handbook
Policy precedence
University and SGAES policies supersede departmental guidance. Students must consult
University calendars and SGAES forms for official deadlines regarding admission, candidacy,
defense scheduling, formatting checks, and graduation.
7
Updates and effective dates
The Department may update this handbook to improve clarity, strengthen alignment with
University policy, or reflect accreditation requirements. Unless otherwise stated, changes
apply prospectively. The Department will communicate material policy changes to students
and advisors.
Terminology
This handbook uses the following conventions.
• “Must” indicates a requirement.
• “Should” indicates a strong recommendation.
• “May” indicates an approved option subject to advisor and GPC approval.
• “Committee” refers to the thesis or dissertation committee unless otherwise specified.
1.8 Roles and responsibilities
Students
Students are responsible for: maintaining full-time engagement with coursework and research;
upholding professional and academic integrity; meeting deadlines; communicating progress;
scheduling required meetings and exams; and ensuring continuous enrollment or approved
leave.
Advisors
Advisors provide mentorship in research design, rigor, and ethics; give timely feedback;
facilitate professional development; and help the student plan and meet milestones. Advisors
set research expectations appropriate to the degree level and ensure students have the training
and resources to progress.
Graduate Program Committee
The GPC oversees admissions processes, monitors student progress in collaboration with
advisors, adjudicates petitions, and ensures fair, consistent application of departmental
policies.
1.9 Paths to support and resolution
Students should first communicate concerns to their advisor. If the concern involves the advisor
or cannot be resolved directly, students should contact the GPC Chair or the Department
Chair. Students may also access University resources for confidential consultation or formal
processes as applicable under University policy.

1.10 Quick-start checklists
New student, before arrival
• Confirm funding, stipend start date, and any onboarding documentation with the
Department or advisor.
• Review program curriculum, typical plans of study, and required trainings (for example,
safety or RCR).
• Contact the advisor regarding first-semester expectations and rotation plans if applicable.
First two weeks
• Complete safety and compliance trainings required by the University and the research
group.
• Meet with the advisor to set expectations, initial goals, and weekly meeting cadence.
• For students on rotations, confirm the rotation schedule and deliverables with the GPC.
First semester
• Draft a plan of study aligned with program requirements and discuss it with the advisor.
• Identify a thesis or dissertation topic area and provisional committee composition.
• Attend departmental seminars and relevant journal clubs.
1.11 Contact and communication
Official departmental communication is sent via University email. Students must check email
regularly and respond in a timely manner. Students should maintain professional standards
in all written and verbal communications and schedule meetings with sufficient lead time.
1.12 Statement on academic integrity and professional
conduct
The Department upholds strict standards for academic integrity and professional conduct,
including responsible scholarship, originality of work, proper attribution, and collegial behavior.
Misconduct is subject to University procedures and penalties. Policies specific to academic
integrity, generative AI, professional conduct, and non-discrimination are detailed later in
this handbook.
1.13 Summary
This handbook is the operational guide for graduate education in the Department of Biological
Sciences. Read it thoroughly, consult it regularly, and partner with your advisor and committee

to plan, execute, and communicate high-quality research. The Department is committed to
your success and to a training environment that is rigorous, inclusive, and supportive.

Chapter 2
Programs and Governance
2.1 Graduate programs
The Department offers three graduate programs. Each program includes advanced coursework,
research training, professional development, and a culminating thesis or dissertation with a
public seminar and committee defense.
• MS in Biological Sciences (thesis)
• MS in Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience (thesis)
• PhD in Neuroscience (dissertation)
MS programs at a glance
• 30 total credits, typically 27 credits of graduate coursework plus 3 credits of thesis
research.
• Designed for completion in approximately 2 years of full-time study, including summers.
• Includes a thesis proposal, a public seminar, and a committee defense.
PhD at a glance
• Minimum 60 total credits, including advanced coursework and dissertation research.
• Qualifying examinations (written and proposal defense), advancement to candidacy, and
a public dissertation defense.
• Professional development and teaching preparation where applicable.
2.2 Program leadership and committees
Graduate Program Committee (GPC)
The GPC oversees admissions, monitors student progress, reviews petitions, and ensures
policy consistency. It recommends policy updates to align with University standards and the
Department’s research mission.
11
Research advisors
Research advisors supervise day-to-day research training and help students plan coursework,
set milestones, and reach timely completion. Advisors are responsible for mentoring aligned
with disciplinary best practices and departmental policies.
Thesis and dissertation committees
Committees provide independent oversight and expertise from within and beyond the De-
partment. Committee composition and appointment processes are detailed in the Rotations,
Mentoring, and Committees chapter. Committees meet at key milestones and, for PhD
students, should meet at least annually after advancement to candidacy.
2.3 Seminars, journal clubs, and departmental commu-
nity
Graduate education is immersed in scholarly exchange. Students are expected to attend
departmental seminars, engage in journal clubs, and contribute to the intellectual life of
the Department. The Department strives to foster a collegial environment that values
collaboration, inclusivity, and scientific rigor.
2.4 Advising and mentoring principles
The Department embraces a mentorship compact that clarifies expectations for communication,
feedback, research workload, authorship ethics, and conflict resolution. Students and advisors
should review and sign the mentor-student agreement early in the program and revisit it
periodically, at minimum during annual reviews.
2.5 Policy alignment
All departmental guidance in this handbook aligns with and defers to University and SGAES
policies on official procedures, deadlines, and degree conferral. Program staff and faculty will
assist students in understanding and meeting those requirements, but students are ultimately
responsible for compliance and on-time submissions to the Graduate School.
2.6 Continuous improvement
The Department evaluates graduate programs through annual reviews, student progress
metrics, and external feedback. Policy refinements are made to strengthen training quality,
maintain fairness and consistency, and support DSU’s research trajectory.

Chapter 3
Admissions and Funding
3.1 Overview
Admission to all graduate programs in the Department of Biological Sciences is competitive
and based on a holistic review of academic preparation, research experience, and potential
for success. Applicants must submit complete applications by posted deadlines and meet the
criteria below. Available space and funding influence admission offers.
3.2 Admission criteria

6.6 Qualifying examinations
Qualifying Exam Part 1 (QE1: written)
QE1 assesses core knowledge, literature analysis, and scientific reasoning across multiple
neuroscience subdisciplines. Students are typically provided a small set of primary research
articles. The exam consists of two written sessions (approximately 5 hours each) administered
on consecutive days in mid-spring of Year 2. Outcomes are:
• Pass.
• Conditional pass with remediation (specified by the QE subcommittee).
• Fail (normally results in dismissal from the PhD program; in limited cases and subject
to approvals, a terminal MS option may be offered).

plan. The student submits a written, grant-style proposal (typically 4 to 10 pages single- to

immediate dissertation scope. After the committee reviews the written proposal, the student
delivers a closed-door oral defense to the committee. Outcomes are:
• Pass.
• Pass with revision or second defense (committee specifies revisions and timeline).
• Fail (normally requires exit from the program; a terminal MS may be offered under
defined conditions).

dissertation proposal, completion of required coursework as specified by the committee, and

should normally occur by the middle of Year 3. Students must maintain continuous enrollment
in appropriate research or dissertation credits after candidacy.

pathways with committee and GPC approval:
• Manuscript-style dissertation composed of multiple, publication-ready chapters.
• Externally evaluated, comprehensive capstone research project conducted with an outside
partner (for example, agency or industry), with independent expert review.
• Patent-focused or applied dissertation documenting a novel, validated technology or
process with supporting experimental evidence.
• Substantial peer-reviewed conference proceedings or extended abstracts, accompanied
by a cohesive written dissertation integrating the contributions.

for originality, rigor, and impact.

PhD training includes professional development and, where assigned, supervised teaching.
BIOL 603 provides foundational pedagogy and is normally completed in Year 3. Students
are expected to participate in departmental seminars, present research in internal forums,
and engage in conferences as appropriate. The Department encourages mentorship of
undergraduate researchers and outreach consistent with DSU’s mission as an HBCU.

• First month: complete safety and compliance trainings; confirm rotation plan (if appli-
cable) and advisor expectations; begin plan of study.

• 3 to 4 months before target defense: confirm Graduate School deadlines; schedule public

Chapter 7
Rotations, Mentoring, and Graduate
Committees
7.1 Purpose and scope
This chapter defines how students rotate through laboratories, establish and sustain mentoring
relationships, and constitute graduate committees. The goal is to ensure rapid lab placement,
clear expectations, rigorous oversight, and timely degree progress consistent with R1 standards
and DSU’s HBCU mission.
7.2 Laboratory rotations
Who rotates
• Institutionally funded students (for example, teaching assistantships) normally complete
first-term rotations prior to permanent lab placement.
• Grant-funded students may join the funding mentor’s lab at matriculation; brief ex-
ploratory rotations are recommended but not required.
Structure and timeline
• Default plan: three rotations during the first semester.
• Typical duration: 4 to 5 weeks per rotation within a standard 15-week term.
• Scheduling: the GPC coordinates a rotation calendar before classes begin; adjustments
are approved by the GPC and communicated to all mentors involved.
Eligibility and prerequisites
Before starting a rotation, students must complete all lab safety, compliance, and facility-
specific onboarding required for the host lab. Regulated work may not begin until approvals
are in place (for example, IACUC, IRB, IBC, radiation, chemical safety).
35
Rotation objectives
Each rotation must provide structured exposure to the lab’s scientific questions, methods,
expectations, and culture. Objectives include acquisition of core techniques, engagement
with group meetings and journal clubs, and a realistic assessment of fit for both student and
mentor.
Deliverables and documentation
For each rotation the student must:
• File a 1 page rotation plan with the GPC within the first week (aims, tasks, expected
outputs, training to be completed).
• Maintain a dated lab notebook with methods, data, and brief interpretations (paper or
electronic per lab policy).
• Submit a rotation summary at the end of the period (maximum 2 pages: aims, activities,
skills learned, preliminary results if any, lessons learned).
• Give a 5 to 7 minute lightning talk to peers and the GPC at the end of the rotation
cycle.
Evaluation and feedback
Mentors provide the GPC a brief evaluation for each rotation addressing preparation, engage-
ment, technical growth, record keeping, and professionalism. The GPC may use a simple
rubric with ratings and comments to standardize feedback across labs.
Matching process
After the rotation cycle:
1. Students submit a ranked list of preferred labs and a short justification.
2. Faculty indicate available capacity and funding constraints.
3. The GPC finalizes placements balancing preference, capacity, funding, and program
needs; decisions are communicated in writing to all parties.
If a match is not achieved after the three rotations, the GPC may authorize an additional
rotation and will work actively to secure a placement. Continued institutional funding is
contingent on timely placement and satisfactory conduct.
Professional expectations during rotations
Students must adhere to lab norms for attendance, communication, and safety; respect data
confidentiality and material transfer restrictions; and credit the host lab appropriately in
any subsequent use of rotation data. Advisors must provide a concise onboarding checklist,
accessible supervision, and timely feedback.
36
7.3 Mentoring framework
Mentor-student agreement (required)
The Department uses a written mentor-student agreement to define expectations for commu-
nication, workload, training, authorship ethics, intellectual property, and conflict resolution.
The agreement must be:
• Reviewed and signed within 30 days of permanent lab placement.
• Revisited at least annually as part of the departmental annual review process.
• Updated when project scope, funding, or committee composition changes materially.
Meeting cadence and communication
• 1 to 1 meetings: weekly by default; adjust cadence by mutual agreement as independence
increases.
• Lab meetings: participate regularly; present progress at least once per term.
• Written updates: brief weekly update email or shared note capturing aims for the week,
blockers, and risks.
• Response expectations: mentors acknowledge substantive student communications within
2 business days or designate alternates when traveling.
Work norms, leave, and availability
• Research intensity varies by project; students and mentors set specific weekly expectations
that respect DSU policies and safety constraints.
• Planned leave (for example, conference travel, vacation) requires advance notice and
coverage planning for shared responsibilities.
• Unplanned leave (for example, illness) should be communicated as soon as practical; the
Department supports students in accessing health and counseling resources.
Rigor, reproducibility, and data stewardship
• Maintain complete, contemporaneous lab notebooks; store raw data, processed data,
and analysis code in lab-approved repositories with routine backup.
• Use rigorous experimental design and appropriate statistics; preregister analyses when
suitable and feasible.
• Document environments for computational work (for example, software versions, scripts,
parameters) to enable reproduction.
• Follow sponsor and University policies on data retention, sharing, and disclosure; consult
the advisor and University offices for guidance on data with privacy, security, or export
control implications.
37
Authorship and contributions
• Discuss authorship expectations at project start and revisit as roles evolve; record
contribution statements in writing.
• Follow disciplinary norms on first and corresponding authorship and avoid honorary or
coercive authorship.
• Resolve authorship disputes first within the lab; if needed, seek confidential guidance
from the GPC or Department Chair.
Professional development
• Prepare and update an Individual Development Plan annually; discuss goals with the
advisor and, where appropriate, the committee.
• Identify opportunities for teaching, mentorship of undergraduates, outreach, internships,
and leadership aligned with career goals.
• Plan conference participation and manuscript submissions strategically with mentor
guidance and funding realities.
Changing advisors
Students may request a change of advisor when needed. The GPC will facilitate transitions
subject to availability of an appropriate mentor and funding. Steps:
1. Meet with the GPC Chair to discuss goals and constraints; the Chair may suggest
mediation if appropriate.
2. Secure written agreement from a prospective new advisor and notify the current advisor.
3. File a committee update with the GPC and any required Graduate School forms.
4. Arrange data and material transfer in accordance with University policy and sponsor
terms.
Students should remain professional throughout; the Department’s priority is student progress
and well-being.
7.4 Graduate committees
Purpose and responsibilities
Graduate committees provide independent oversight, broad expertise, and mentoring beyond
the primary advisor. Core responsibilities include:
• Reviewing and approving the plan of study, proposal, and any major scope changes.
• Advising on experimental design, feasibility, risks, and ethical compliance.
• Evaluating candidacy milestones, thesis or dissertation quality, and defense outcomes.
• Meeting at least annually after candidacy (PhD) to track progress and adjust timelines.
Composition and appointment
MS committees. At least 4 members:
38
• Primary research advisor (chair).
• At least 2 additional DSU Biology graduate faculty.
• At least 1 member from outside the Department of Biological Sciences.
PhD committees. At least 5 members:
• Primary research advisor (chair).
• At least 3 additional DSU Biology graduate faculty.
• At least 1 external member from outside the Department; external to the University is
encouraged when appropriate.
Timeline.
• MS: form by end of Year 1 or earlier when feasible.
• PhD: form by end of Year 1; approve formally at the start of Year 2 and before qualifying
examinations.
Appointments are reviewed by the GPC for alignment with expertise and policy.
Conduct of meetings
• Frequency: for PhD students, at least annually after candidacy; for MS students, at
least at proposal approval and prior to defense. Additional meetings are encouraged at
key inflection points.
• Agenda: student circulates a concise written update 5 business days in advance (progress,
data, roadblocks, next aims, timeline). The advisor ensures the agenda covers risks,
resources, and decisions needed.
• Minutes: student provides brief minutes with decisions, action items, and deadlines;
advisor verifies accuracy; minutes are shared with the committee and retained by the
student and advisor.
• Quorum: a majority of committee members including the advisor and at least one
external member should participate; remote attendance is permitted via reliable video
conferencing.
Qualifying exams and proposal defenses
• QE1 (PhD written exam) is administered by a designated subcommittee; grading uses a
rubric with outcomes defined in the program chapter.
• QE2 (PhD proposal) is defended orally before the dissertation committee after submission
of a written proposal per program guidelines.
• MS proposal defenses are closed meetings of the thesis committee following circulation
of a written proposal.
Changes to committee membership
Committee composition may be updated due to expertise needs, availability, or conflicts.
Process:
1. Consult the advisor and proposed new member(s).
39
2. Submit a request to the GPC detailing rationale and confirming willingness of the new
member(s).
3. File any required Graduate School forms by posted deadlines.
If a member becomes unavailable for an extended period, the student and advisor must
initiate a replacement to prevent delays.
Conflicts of interest and confidentiality
Members disclose potential conflicts of interest (for example, close personal or financial
relationships) to the advisor and GPC; remedies may include recusal from specific decisions
or replacement. Committee deliberations are confidential; materials are not to be shared
beyond the committee without explicit consent.
7.5 Documentation and required records
Students and advisors must maintain the following, as applicable:
• Plan of study approved by the advisor and committee.
• Mentor-student agreement (initial and annual updates).
• Rotation plans, summaries, and mentor evaluations.
• Annual review self-assessment and advisor evaluation; for PhD, annual committee
meeting minutes after candidacy.
• Compliance approvals (for example, IACUC, IRB, IBC) and required safety training
records.
• Proposal, candidacy, defense, and graduation forms required by the Graduate School.
Templates and forms are provided in the appendices or via the Department’s online portal.
7.6 Checklists
Rotation kickoff (each rotation)
• Safety and compliance onboarding complete for the host lab.
• 1 page rotation plan filed with the GPC and host mentor.
• Access to facilities, data storage, and notebook platform confirmed.
• Meeting schedule with host mentor established.
Rotation closeout (each rotation)
• Notebook up to date; raw data and code stored in lab repository.
• 2 page rotation summary submitted to the GPC and host mentor.
• Lightning talk delivered at the rotation symposium.
• Materials and credentials returned or deactivated per lab policy.
40
Advisor-student 30-60-90 day plan (post-placement)
• 30 days: finalize mentor-student agreement; align aims and training plan; set weekly
meeting cadence; confirm data management practices.
• 60 days: complete early milestones (for example, pilot experiments, pipeline setup);
identify committee candidates; map proposal timeline.
• 90 days: submit plan of study for advisor approval; draft proposal outline and figures;
schedule committee formation.
Committee formation
• Confirm membership meets program requirements and expertise needs.
• Secure written agreement from all members; submit to the GPC for approval.
• File Graduate School forms per deadlines.
• Schedule the first committee meeting and circulate a brief project overview.
7.7 Standards and accountability
The Department expects professional, inclusive conduct from all participants in graduate
training. When expectations are not met, the GPC may implement remedial actions, modify
funding, or recommend program separation consistent with University policy. Students and
mentors are encouraged to seek early advice from the GPC or Department Chair to resolve
concerns promptly and maintain momentum toward degree completion.

Chapter 8
Progress, Evaluations, and Good
Standing
8.1 Purpose
This chapter defines how the Department monitors academic and research progress, evaluates
performance, and maintains consistent standards for good standing. The goals are to support
timely degree completion, uphold R1-level rigor, and ensure fair, transparent processes
consistent with University policy.
8.2 Definition of good standing
A graduate student is in good standing when all of the following are true:
• Academics: cumulative GPA is at least 3.0 on a 4.0 scale; grades in core and foundation
courses are normally B or higher.
• Research: satisfactory progress toward the approved plan of study, proposal aims, and
degree milestones as judged by the advisor and, where applicable, the committee.
• Conduct: professional behavior consistent with departmental and University policies
(for example, academic integrity, safety, Title IX and EEO compliance).
• Enrollment: continuous enrollment each fall and spring or an approved leave of absence;
sustaining registration after completing required credits until final approval.
• Assistantship performance: when funded, satisfactory fulfillment of TA/RA duties
and timely completion of required trainings.
8.3 Academic standards
GPA and grades
• Minimum cumulative GPA of 3.0 is required for continued enrollment and graduation.
• Core and foundation courses normally require grades of B or higher.
42
• Earning two grades of C (or below) or falling below the minimum GPA may trigger
probation, loss of departmental funding, or dismissal in accordance with University
policy.
Credit load and registration
• Register each term in coursework, research, dissertation, or sustaining status as appro-
priate to degree stage.
• Students receiving assistantships must meet full-time registration requirements set by
the Graduate School.
Transfer credit
Up to 9 graduate credits (grade B or higher) from accredited institutions may be counted with
advisor, GPC, and Graduate School approval. Courses must align with the DSU curriculum
and the approved plan of study.
8.4 Research progress expectations
Planning and communication
• Maintain an advisor-approved plan of study and a living project plan with aims, mile-
stones, risks, and timelines.
• Meet regularly with the advisor (for example, weekly) and keep written notes of decisions
and action items.
• Participate in lab meetings, seminars, and journal clubs; present progress at least once
per term.
Rigor and reproducibility
• Maintain complete, contemporaneous research records (notebooks, raw data, analysis
code) in lab-approved repositories with appropriate backup.
• Use sound experimental design, proper controls, and appropriate statistics; document
analysis environments and parameters for reproducibility.
• Complete all required compliance approvals (for example, IACUC, IRB, IBC) before
initiating regulated work; complete safety trainings prior to lab activities.
Deliverables by stage
Pre-proposal (MS and PhD). Literature synthesis, pilot data, feasibility analyses, and
a written proposal outline with figures and timelines.
Post-proposal (MS). Execution of approved aims; interim presentations; draft thesis
chapters; public seminar and defense preparation.
43
Candidacy/post-proposal (PhD). Execution and refinement of aims; manuscript draft-
ing and submission; annual committee meetings; dissertation outline and figures.
8.5 Annual review (all graduate students)
Purpose and timing
An annual review is conducted each summer to assess progress, set goals, and align ex-
pectations. The process documents achievements, identifies risks, and, if needed, initiates
remediation.
Components
• Student self-assessment: accomplishments, skills gained, research summary, presenta-
tions/publications, updated goals, and anticipated timeline to degree.
• Advisor evaluation: performance in research, professionalism, communication, record
keeping, safety and compliance, and assistantship duties; specific feedback and recom-
mendations.
• Committee engagement: for PhD students after candidacy, an annual committee
meeting is expected; minutes should summarize progress, decisions, and next steps.
Outcomes
• Satisfactory: on track with clear next goals.
• Satisfactory with recommendations: minor adjustments advisable; follow-up at the
next regular check-in.
• Needs improvement (remediation): written plan with concrete milestones, resources,
and dates.
• Unsatisfactory: serious deficiencies; probation or funding modification may be recom-
mended; dismissal may be considered for persistent noncompliance or misconduct.
Documentation
The Department maintains the student self-assessment, advisor evaluation, any committee
minutes, and any remediation plan. Students and advisors retain copies. Required forms and
templates are provided in the appendices or via the departmental portal.
8.6 Assistantships: expectations and evaluation
Teaching assistantships (TAs)
• Complete required pedagogy and safety training before assignment; adhere to course
lead instructions and timelines.
44
• Typical duties may include laboratory preparation, instruction, grading, office hours,
and proctoring; workload is set by the Department consistent with University policy.
• Performance is evaluated each term by the course supervisor and informs funding
continuation decisions.
Research assistantships (RAs)
• RA duties are defined by the advisor and sponsor scope; expectations include reliable
effort, accurate records, and deliverables aligned with project milestones.
• Funded students must obtain written approval from the advisor, GPC, and Department
Chair before accepting outside employment.
8.7 Remediation and probation
Triggers
Common triggers include: cumulative GPA below 3.0; multiple grades of C or below; missed
proposal or exam deadlines; inadequate research progress; failure to meet compliance or safety
obligations; unprofessional conduct.
Remediation plan
When remediation is warranted, the advisor (and committee where applicable) drafts a
written plan that:
• Defines specific deficiencies and the objective criteria for success.
• Lists concrete actions, resources, and support.
• Sets a timeline with checkpoints (typically 30, 60, and 90 days).
• States consequences if milestones are not met (for example, probation, funding modifica-
tion, program separation).
The student, advisor, and GPC sign the plan; progress is monitored at scheduled checkpoints.
Probation
If deficiencies persist or are severe, the Department may place the student on probation. The
probation letter specifies conditions, timelines, and consequences. Failure to satisfy probation
terms may result in loss of funding or dismissal consistent with University procedures.
8.8 Dismissal and appeals
Dismissal
Grounds for dismissal include sustained unsatisfactory progress, academic dishonesty, egre-
gious safety violations, or professional misconduct. Dismissal recommendations originate
45
from the advisor and GPC and are reviewed by the Department Chair under University
policy.
Appeals
Students may appeal adverse decisions following departmental and Graduate School proce-
dures. Typical steps are: written appeal to the Department Chair within the stated window;
if unresolved, appeal to College leadership or the Graduate School as specified by University
policy.

Chapter 9
Milestones, Candidacy, and
Examinations
9.1 Purpose
This chapter defines the required academic milestones for MS and PhD students, the standards
and logistics for qualifying examinations and proposal defenses, the advancement-to-candidacy
process, and the procedures for thesis and dissertation defenses. Policies are aligned with
University and SGAES requirements and calibrated to R1 expectations while honoring DSU’s
mission as an HBCU.
9.2 Milestone map (overview)
Master of Science
1. Plan of study approved by advisor.
2. Thesis committee formed and approved.
3. Written thesis proposal and closed proposal defense.
4. Advancement to candidacy paperwork filed with Graduate School.
5. Thesis research and writing; interim presentations as assigned.
6. Public seminar and thesis defense; outcomes recorded.
7. Final revisions and thesis submission per SGAES formatting and deadlines.
8. Degree conferral upon final approvals; continuous enrollment required until conferral.
Doctor of Philosophy
1. Rotations (if institutionally funded) and permanent lab placement.
2. Dissertation committee formed and approved.
3. Qualifying Exam Part 1 (QE1, written).
4. Qualifying Exam Part 2 (QE2, proposal: written document and oral defense).
5. Advancement to candidacy upon passing QE1 and QE2 with approvals filed.
6. Dissertation research; scholarly output to peer-reviewed standards.
49
7. Public seminar and dissertation defense; outcomes recorded.

9.3 Master of Science milestones (details)
Plan of study
Students draft a plan of study in the first semester with the advisor, listing foundations,
electives, BIOL 505, professional development, and thesis research credits. The plan should
articulate coherence with the thesis area and include a targeted timeline to candidacy and
defense.
Thesis committee
By the end of Year 1 (earlier when feasible), form a committee of at least four members:
primary advisor (chair), two additional DSU Biology graduate faculty, and one member from
outside the Department. Submit for departmental approval.
Thesis proposal and defense
Document. 10 to 15 pages excluding references and appendices. Recommended structure:
• Specific aims (1 page).
• Background and significance (context and gap).
• Preliminary results (if available).
• Approach and methods (design, controls, reagents, facilities).
• Analysis plan (statistics, power where applicable, software).
• Rigor and reproducibility (blinding, randomization, replication).
• Risks and alternatives (contingency plans).
• Timeline and milestones.
• Compliance and safety notes (IACUC, IRB, IBC as relevant).
Circulation. Provide the complete document to the committee at least 2 weeks before the
proposal defense (3 weeks if required by University policy).
Oral defense. Closed meeting (committee and student). Outcome options: approve;
approve with revisions; revise and resubmit.
Advancement to candidacy (MS)
File Graduate School candidacy paperwork after committee approval of the proposal. Candi-
dacy is required before scheduling the thesis defense.
50
Thesis defense and submission
Public seminar. Approximately 1 hour with Q and A for the audience.
Closed defense. Committee examination immediately follows the seminar. Outcomes:
accept; accept with revisions; revise and resubmit; revise with second defense; fail.
Submission. Complete revisions and submit the final thesis and required forms by SGAES
deadlines. Maintain enrollment (thesis or sustaining) until final approval.
9.4 Doctor of Philosophy milestones (details)
Committee formation
By the end of Year 1, form a dissertation committee of at least five members: primary advisor
(chair), three additional DSU Biology graduate faculty, and at least one external member
from outside the Department (external to the University encouraged when appropriate).
Submit for departmental approval.
Qualifying Exam Part 1 (QE1: written)
Purpose. Assess foundational knowledge, literature analysis, and scientific reasoning across
neuroscience subdisciplines.
Format. Two written sessions (approximately 5 hours each) administered on consecutive
days in mid-spring of Year 2, based on a small set of assigned primary research articles.
Standards. Independent work; no collaboration; only materials authorized by the QE
subcommittee are permitted.
Outcomes.
• Pass.
• Conditional pass with remediation (specific written or oral follow-up, reading list, or
targeted assignment).
• Fail (normally results in dismissal from the PhD program; in limited circumstances, a
terminal MS option may be offered subject to approvals).
Qualifying Exam Part 2 (QE2: proposal)
Purpose. Evaluate the student’s capacity to formulate, justify, and defend an independent
research plan at the doctoral level.
51
Written proposal. 4 to 10 pages single- to 1.5-spaced (excluding references), grant-style.
Required elements:
• Specific aims, including at least one aim extending beyond the immediate dissertation
scope.
• Significance and innovation.
• Approach (design, methods, expected results, interpretation, pitfalls, alternatives).
• Analysis plan (statistics, power where appropriate, software and computational environ-
ment).
• Rigor and reproducibility; data management and sharing plan as appropriate.
• Compliance and safety considerations.
• Timeline and milestones.
Circulation. Provide the complete proposal to the committee at least 2 weeks before the
QE2 defense (3 weeks if required by University policy).
Oral defense. Closed meeting with the dissertation committee. Outcomes:
• Pass.
• Pass with revisions or second defense (committee specifies required changes and timeline).
• Fail (normally requires exit from the PhD; a terminal MS may be offered under defined
conditions).
Advancement to candidacy (PhD)
Advance upon passing QE1 and QE2, with committee-approved proposal and completed
candidacy paperwork filed by Graduate School deadlines. Advancement should normally
occur by the middle of Year 3. Continuous enrollment in dissertation or sustaining status is
required after candidacy.
Scholarly output expectation
Before scheduling the dissertation defense, students must present evidence of significant,
original contribution to the field, typically at least one first-authored, peer-reviewed journal
article accepted or an approved equivalent (for example, manuscript-style dissertation with
publication-ready chapters) as authorized by the committee and GPC.
Dissertation defense and submission
Public seminar. Approximately 1 hour with audience Q and A.
Closed defense. Committee examination immediately follows.
Outcomes. Accept; accept with revisions; revise and resubmit; revise with second defense;
fail.
52
Submission. Complete revisions and submit the final dissertation and all forms per SGAES
deadlines; maintain enrollment until all approvals are final.
9.5 Examination and defense logistics
Scheduling
• Coordinate proposed dates with the advisor and committee at least 4 weeks in advance.
• Confirm room or virtual platform and any required equipment at least 2 weeks in
advance.
• For public defenses, notify the Department for seminar announcement at least 1 week in
advance.
• File required Graduate School scheduling forms by posted deadlines.
Materials and format
• Written documents (proposal, thesis, dissertation) must be complete drafts, with figures
and references, not outlines.
• Use consistent citation format and approved figure and table labeling.
• Follow SGAES formatting for margins, pagination, title page, abstract, and acknowledg-
ments.
Accessibility and accommodations
Students requiring accommodations should work with University accessibility services; inform
the advisor and GPC early to ensure equitable exam conditions.
Academic integrity
All exams and defenses are governed by University academic integrity policy. Unauthorized
collaboration, plagiarism, or misrepresentation may result in exam failure, probation, funding
loss, or dismissal.
Remote participation
Committee members may participate via reliable video conferencing. The chair is responsible
for verifying identity, ensuring secure document access, and maintaining examination integrity.

QE2
Committees may permit a revision or a second defense within a specified window. A fail
typically requires exit from the PhD program; a terminal MS may be offered under defined
conditions and approvals.
Proposal (MS)
Committees may require revision and a repeat proposal meeting. Repeated failure to pass
the proposal may result in probation or program separation.
Appeals
Students may appeal adverse decisions following departmental and Graduate School proce-
dures and timelines.
9.8 Checklists
MS proposal defense
• Confirm committee membership and availability; schedule date and room.
• Circulate complete proposal at least 2 weeks in advance.
• Bring updated plan of study and compliance status summary.
• After defense: record outcome; complete revisions; file candidacy paperwork.
PhD QE1
• Confirm exam dates and authorized materials; review policy on integrity.
• Prepare literature notes; practice timed analysis and synthesis.
• After exam: monitor outcome; complete any remediation assigned.
55
PhD QE2
• Confirm committee and schedule; circulate proposal at least 2 weeks in advance.
• Prepare a concise oral presentation (for example, 20 to 30 minutes).
• After defense: complete revisions; file candidacy paperwork upon pass.
Thesis/dissertation defense
• Verify eligibility: candidacy, credits, compliance, scholarly output (PhD).
• Schedule seminar and closed defense; announce public seminar.
• Deliver complete document to committee at least 2 weeks in advance.
• Post-defense: complete revisions; submit final document and forms by SGAES deadlines;
maintain enrollment until conferral.
9.9 Summary
Milestones and examinations mark readiness for independent research and degree completion.
This chapter consolidates standards, logistics, and rubrics to promote clarity, fairness, and
rigor. Students, advisors, and committees should use these guidelines alongside University
and SGAES policies to plan and execute each stage without delay.

Chapter 10
Defense, Submission, and Degree
Conferral
10.1 Purpose
This chapter defines the end-to-end process for thesis and dissertation defenses, post-defense
revisions, final submission to the Graduate School, and degree conferral. Policies herein align
with University and SGAES requirements. When conflicts arise, University and SGAES
policies take precedence.
10.2 Eligibility to defend
Students may schedule a defense when all of the following are satisfied.
Master of Science
• Good standing: cumulative GPA at least 3.0; required coursework substantially complete.
• Committee: approved committee on file; committee membership current.
• Proposal and candidacy: thesis proposal approved; candidacy paperwork filed with the
Graduate School.
• Research: scope sufficient for a defensible thesis; advisor authorizes scheduling.
• Compliance: all required approvals complete (for example, IACUC, IRB, IBC) and in
good standing; safety training current.
• Administrative: continuous enrollment or approved leave; student has applied for gradu-
ation per Graduate School deadlines.
Doctor of Philosophy
• Good standing: cumulative GPA at least 3.0; required coursework complete or on track
per committee.
• Committee: approved dissertation committee on file; committee membership current.
57
• Candidacy: passed QE1 and QE2; candidacy approved and filed with the Graduate
School.
• Scholarly output: evidence of publishable-quality research per program policy and
committee expectations (for example, at least one first-authored peer-reviewed manuscript
accepted or an approved equivalent).
• Compliance: all required approvals complete and current; data management and safety
practices verified.
• Administrative: continuous enrollment or approved leave; student has applied for gradu-
ation per Graduate School deadlines.
10.3 Scheduling the defense
Timeline
• 8 to 12 weeks prior: consult advisor and committee on readiness and proposed dates;
confirm Graduate School deadlines for the intended term.
• 4 to 6 weeks prior: secure room or virtual platform; file internal scheduling notice with
the Department; initiate Graduate School scheduling forms if required.
• 2 to 3 weeks prior: distribute complete draft to the committee; confirm audiovisual needs
and access for remote participants.
Format
A defense consists of a public seminar followed immediately by a closed examination with the
committee. Remote participation is permitted with reliable video conferencing and identity
verification. The advisor (chair) ensures examination integrity and attendance by a quorum
of committee members.
Announcement
Public defenses must be announced to the Department (and, where required, to the Graduate
School) at least 1 week in advance. Announcements include title, abstract, date, time, location
or link, and student and advisor names.
10.4 The public seminar
• Duration: approximately 45 to 60 minutes for the presentation, followed by audience
questions as time allows.
• Scope: background and significance; aims; methods; results; interpretation; limitations;
future directions; broader impacts.
• Accessibility: ensure figures are legible; define abbreviations; practice inclusive, profes-
sional communication.
58
10.5 The closed defense
Conduct
The committee examines the candidate on the thesis or dissertation and the underlying
science. The chair manages time, ensures equitable questioning, and maintains a professional,
constructive tone. After questioning, the candidate is excused for committee deliberation.
Outcomes
• Accept without changes: all members sign immediately.
• Accept with revisions: advisor or committee verifies completion of revisions prior to final
signatures.
• Revise and resubmit: substantial revisions required; committee re-reviews prior to
signatures.
• Revise with second defense: significant re-examination required after revision.
• Fail: document does not meet degree standards; committee communicates rationale and
recommended next steps.
The chair records the outcome on the appropriate departmental and Graduate School forms.
10.6 Document standards and formatting
General
• The version circulated to the committee for defense must be a complete, formatted draft
with all chapters, figures, tables, citations, and appendices.
• University and SGAES formatting requirements govern title page, abstract, pagination,
margins, headings, figure and table placement, and citation style. Where this handbook
and University guidance differ, follow University guidance.
Styles and citations
Use a consistent citation format approved by the advisor and committee. Verify that all
references cited in the text appear in the bibliography, and that all entries are complete and
correctly formatted.
Figures, tables, and data
• Provide high-resolution figures with readable labels; ensure color choices remain inter-
pretable when printed in grayscale.
• Ensure that every figure and table has an informative caption and is cited in the text.
• Where data are subject to privacy, export control, or sponsor restrictions, coordinate
with the advisor and University offices before submission.
59
10.7 Authorship, copyright, and embargo
Prior publications
For manuscript-style theses or dissertations, clearly indicate which chapters correspond to
published or submitted works and list co-authors. The candidate must be the primary
contributor for doctoral work unless otherwise approved by the committee.
Permissions
If reusing published material (for example, figures, tables, or substantial text), secure publisher
permissions as required. Maintain documentation of permissions for Graduate School review.
Embargo
Embargo requests, when permitted by the Graduate School, must be justified (for example,
pending patents or sensitive sponsor obligations) and approved before final submission.
Typical embargo periods, if available, are defined by the Graduate School.
10.8 Data, code, and research records
• Archive raw data, processed data, and analysis code in advisor- or department-approved
repositories prior to leaving DSU, consistent with sponsor and University policies.
• Document software versions, parameters, and workflows sufficient for reproduction.
• Transfer custody of shared materials (for example, cell lines, plasmids, animals, instru-
ments, notebooks) as directed by the advisor and University policy.
10.9 Post-defense revisions and approvals
Revisions
Complete required revisions promptly. The advisor verifies minor revisions; the full committee
reviews substantial changes. Meet any deadlines specified by the committee or Graduate
School.
Signatures
Collect required signatures on final approval pages using Graduate School formats. Electronic
signatures may be permitted; follow Graduate School guidance.
60
10.10 Final submission and graduation
Submission package
Follow Graduate School instructions for electronic submission (ETD) or other required
formats. A typical package includes:
• Final, committee-approved thesis or dissertation in the required file format.
• Approval and signature pages per Graduate School specifications.
• Required forms (for example, copyright, embargo, survey confirmations).
• Evidence of compliance with formatting checks, if required.
Deadlines
All final documents and forms must be submitted by Graduate School deadlines for the
intended graduation term. Students must remain enrolled (thesis, dissertation, or sustaining
status) until all approvals are final.
Fees and holds
Resolve outstanding fees, library obligations, and equipment returns. Administrative holds
can delay conferral.
10.11 Degree conferral
The degree is conferred in the term when all academic, administrative, and financial require-
ments are complete, and final approvals are posted by the Graduate School. Official conferral
dates and diploma issuance follow University schedules.
10.12 Exit and transition
• Complete University exit surveys and departmental questionnaires.
• Return keys, badges, computing assets, and other University property.
• Coordinate with the advisor on ongoing manuscripts, data requests, and material
transfers.
• Update professional profiles (for example, ORCID, CV) and share current contact
information with the Department for alumni engagement.
10.13 Checklists
MS pre-defense
• Advisor confirms readiness; committee membership current.
• Apply for graduation; confirm Graduate School deadlines.
• Schedule room or virtual platform; announce public seminar.
61
• Circulate complete thesis draft at least 2 weeks prior.
• Verify compliance approvals and training are current.
PhD pre-defense
• Advisor confirms readiness; candidacy on file; scholarly output requirement satisfied or
approved equivalent documented.
• Apply for graduation; confirm Graduate School deadlines.
• Schedule room or virtual platform; announce public seminar.
• Circulate complete dissertation draft at least 2 weeks prior.
• Verify compliance approvals, data archive plan, and authorship attributions.
Day of defense
• Test audiovisual setup and recording if applicable.
• Bring copy of approval pages and required forms.
• Chair reviews procedure and outcomes rubric with committee.
Post-defense
• Complete revisions per committee instructions; secure required signatures.
• Submit final document and forms by Graduate School deadlines.
• Archive data and code; return University property; complete exit surveys.
10.14 Summary
Defenses and final submissions are the culminating steps of graduate training. Plan early,
communicate clearly with your advisor and committee, and adhere to Graduate School
requirements. Continuous enrollment is required until all approvals are complete and the
degree is officially conferred.

Chapter 11
Integrity, Generative AI, Professional
Conduct, and DEI
11.1 Purpose and scope
This chapter codifies standards for academic integrity, responsible conduct of research,
permitted and prohibited uses of generative AI, professional and social conduct, and the
Department’s commitments to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Policies align with
University and SGAES requirements; where conflicts arise, University policy prevails.
11.2 Academic integrity
Expectations
Graduate education requires honesty, originality, and accountability in all scholarly and
professional activities. The following are prohibited:
• Cheating on quizzes, exams, or assignments; unauthorized access to exam materials.
• Plagiarism, including the reuse of text, figures, or code without proper attribution, and
the use of ghostwriting services.
• Unauthorized collaboration or the use of unapproved resources.
• Fabrication or falsification of data, methods, analyses, or approvals.
• Misrepresentation of authorship, contributions, or prior work.
Coursework and exams
Syllabi specify allowed resources and collaboration. When in doubt, ask the instructor before
using any external tool, dataset, or prior solution. Take-home exams and comprehensive
exams are individual unless explicitly stated otherwise.
63
Research and scholarship
Research records must be complete, contemporaneous, and accurate. Selective reporting,
inappropriate image manipulation, undisclosed data exclusions, or unapproved reuse of prior
data are integrity violations. All regulated work requires prior and current approvals.
Procedures and outcomes
Suspected violations are documented by the instructor or advisor and referred to the Graduate
Program Committee (GPC) for review. Outcomes may include remediation, a failing grade,
probation, loss of funding, removal from the advisor’s lab, suspension, or dismissal consistent
with University policy. Records of violations are maintained by the Department as required.
Appeals
A student may appeal an adverse decision to the Department Chair within the published
window. If unresolved, appeals may be made to College leadership or the Graduate School
per University procedures.
11.3 Responsible conduct of research (RCR)
Training and compliance
All graduate students must complete required RCR, safety, and compliance trainings early in
the program and maintain currency. Regulated work may not begin until approvals are in
place.
• Human subjects: IRB approval and human subjects training.
• Vertebrate animals: IACUC protocol approval and animal care training.
• Biohazards and rDNA: IBC approval and biosafety training.
• Chemical, radiation, and laser safety as applicable.
Authorship and contributorship
Discuss authorship at project start and revise as roles evolve. Contributions must justify
authorship; honorary authorship is prohibited. Use written contribution statements when
submitting manuscripts.
Data stewardship
Maintain raw data, processed data, analysis scripts, and lab notebooks in advisor-approved
repositories with backup. Use version control for code. Follow sponsor and University policies
for retention, sharing, privacy, and security. Identify restricted or export-controlled data and
consult the advisor and University offices as needed.
64
Conflicts of interest and commitment
Disclose personal, financial, or professional interests that could influence research or teaching.
Outside employment by funded students requires prior written approval from the advisor,
the GPC, and the Department Chair.
Open science and dissemination
When consistent with policy and sponsor terms, students are encouraged to present at
conferences, post preprints with advisor approval, and share data and code that support
reproducibility. Coordinate embargoes for theses and dissertations with the Graduate School
when needed.
11.4 Use of generative AI
Principles
Generative AI tools can assist research and learning when used transparently and responsibly.
Misuse undermines integrity.
• Permission first: for all graded coursework and for research writing intended for submis-
sion, obtain explicit permission from the instructor or advisor before using AI tools.
• Disclose use: if permitted, disclose where and how AI contributed (for example, drafting,
summarizing, coding suggestions, figure generation).
• Verify and cite: independently verify all AI outputs; correct inaccuracies; do not use
fabricated references; cite primary sources actually consulted.
• Protect confidentiality: do not upload proprietary, unpublished, or regulated information
into external tools without written approval and appropriate data agreements.
• Own your work: final claims, analyses, and interpretations must be the student’s; AI
cannot substitute for original scholarly contribution.
Allowed examples (with permission)
• Brainstorming outlines or alternative phrasings for non-assessed drafts.
• Generating code snippets that the student understands, tests, documents, and cites
appropriately.
• Summarizing literature the student has read, with verification against original sources.
Prohibited examples
• Submitting AI-generated text as original work without disclosure and permission.
• Using AI to complete exams, qualifying exams, or assignments that forbid external
assistance.
• Fabricating citations or claiming results not supported by data.
• Uploading confidential data, unpublished manuscripts, or restricted protocols to public
AI services without authorization.
65
Suggested disclosure language
Include a brief note such as: ”Portions of the text were drafted with an AI-assisted tool and
then verified and revised by the author. All citations were checked against primary sources.”
In manuscripts, follow journal policies.
11.5 Professional and social conduct
Standards
Graduate students represent the Department, College, and University. Expected conduct
includes:
• Treating peers, faculty, staff, and collaborators with courtesy and respect.
• Maintaining professional communication and meeting commitments.
• Following laboratory and field safety policies and promptly reporting incidents.
• Respecting property, facilities, and shared resources.
Harassment, discrimination, and Title IX
Harassment, discrimination, or retaliation on the basis of protected characteristics is prohibited.
Students must comply with Title IX and EEO policies. Report concerns to the Department,
the GPC Chair, or University offices as appropriate. The Department will support referrals
and protect against retaliation consistent with University policy.
Accessibility and accommodations
Students who need disability-related accommodations should contact University accessibility
services. Students should inform instructors and advisors early to enable equitable academic
and research participation.
Digital and public communications
When communicating on behalf of the University or about research affiliated with the
University:
• Protect confidential information and intellectual property.
• Follow sponsor and journal embargoes.
• Use professional tone in public forums and social media; clarify personal opinions are
your own.
11.6 Teaching and TA conduct
Expectations
Teaching assistants must complete required pedagogy and safety trainings, follow course lead
guidelines, and uphold fairness and confidentiality in grading. Communicate schedules, office
66
hours, and grading timelines clearly.
FERPA and student data
Protect student educational records and grades; use approved platforms for course communi-
cations and submissions. Do not store student data on personal devices without appropriate
safeguards.
Academic integrity in teaching
Report suspected academic dishonesty through established procedures. Do not use undisclosed
AI tools for grading or feedback when prohibited by the course lead.
11.7 Conflict resolution and grievances
Pathways
Most concerns can be resolved through early, respectful conversation.
1. Discuss with the primary advisor or course instructor.
2. If unresolved or if the concern involves the advisor, contact the GPC Chair or the
Department Chair.
3. For formal grievances or confidential consultation, use University resources as specified
by Graduate School policy.
4. For harassment or discrimination, report to the University’s Title IX or EEO office per
University procedures.
The Department supports nonretaliation and will help students navigate appropriate processes.
Changing advisors
Students may request a change of advisor for academic or professional reasons. The GPC
facilitates transitions subject to mentor availability and funding. Students and advisors must
agree on data and material transfer consistent with University and sponsor policies.
11.8 DEI commitments and community norms
Commitment
As an HBCU, DSU is committed to a learning community where all members are respected,
supported, and empowered. The Department values diverse perspectives and actively works
to broaden participation in the life sciences.
Inclusive practices
• Use inclusive, respectful language; honor names and pronouns.
67
• Design accessible meetings and materials; post slides in advance when feasible.
• Share opportunities equitably; avoid gatekeeping of resources or information.
• Intervene constructively when witnessing bias or exclusion; seek guidance when needed.
Well-being and support
Students are encouraged to access University health, counseling, and wellness resources. The
Department values work-life balance and will reasonably accommodate religious observances
and caregiving responsibilities consistent with University policy.
11.9 Checklists
Integrity readiness
• Completed RCR and safety trainings; approvals on file for regulated work.
• Lab notebook and data repository set up with backup.
• Agreed authorship and data management expectations documented.
AI usage checklist
• Is AI use permitted for this task by the instructor or advisor?
• Is the contribution disclosed, verified, and properly cited?
• Are confidentiality and data sharing restrictions respected?
TA conduct checklist
• Completed pedagogy orientation and safety training.
• Posted office hours; grading rubric and timelines aligned with course lead.
• FERPA-compliant handling of student records and grades.
Conflict resolution
• Document the concern and steps taken to resolve it.
• Engage advisor or instructor; if unresolved, contact GPC Chair or Department Chair.
• Seek University resources for formal grievances or Title IX/EEO matters.
11.10 Summary
Integrity, professionalism, and inclusion are nonnegotiable foundations of graduate training.
The Department provides clear expectations and support; students and mentors share respon-
sibility for fostering a rigorous, respectful, and inclusive research and learning community.
68
Chapter 12
Teaching, Seminars, and Career
Development
12.1 Purpose
This chapter defines expectations and support for graduate student teaching, participation in
seminars and journal clubs, and structured career development. Policies align with University
requirements and program goals at an R1 standard while reflecting DSU’s HBCU mission.
12.2 Teaching and TA preparation
Teaching philosophy
Teaching is integral to scholarly formation. Graduate students develop communication,
leadership, and mentoring skills through supervised instruction, aligned with evidence-based
pedagogy and inclusive practices.
Requirements
• PhD: complete BIOL 603 Strategies for Effective Teaching in Biology (1 credit) with
supervised teaching experience. Students with prior formal teaching may request a
waiver from the Department Chair with supporting documentation.
• MS: teaching assistantships may be assigned based on departmental needs and student
preparation; when assigned, expectations and training below apply.
TA eligibility and training
• Good academic standing and timely completion of safety and compliance trainings
required for assigned courses or labs.
• Completion of pedagogy orientation or modules designated by the Department or College
prior to first assignment.
69
• Familiarity with course syllabus, grading rubrics, laboratory safety procedures, accessi-
bility policies, and FERPA requirements before instruction begins.
Typical TA duties
• Laboratory setup, safety checks, instruction, and teardown.
• Grading with transparent rubrics; timely and constructive feedback.
• Scheduled office hours and responsive communication on approved platforms.
• Proctoring exams; academic integrity monitoring and reporting.
Workload and supervision
• Workload is calibrated to University policy for assistantships. Course leads define specific
weekly expectations and blackout dates.
• TAs meet routinely with the course lead to plan sessions, align grading standards, and
debrief issues.
• Performance is evaluated each term by the course lead using a departmental rubric;
results inform funding decisions and professional development plans.
Professional and ethical standards
• Maintain impartiality, confidentiality, and professionalism in all student interactions.
• Use accessible materials and inclusive instructional practices.
• Do not use undisclosed AI or external services for grading if prohibited by the course
lead.
• Promptly report accidents, safety incidents, or suspected academic dishonesty following
departmental procedures.
12.3 Seminars, journal clubs, and scholarly engagement
Departmental seminar
• Graduate students are expected to attend seminars organized by or affiliated to the
department. These include department seminars, student thesis presentations, job talks,
college or research center sponsored seminar series, throughout their enrollment.
• Students present their research at least once during the program: MS normally during
Year 2; PhD at least annually after candidacy or as directed by the committee.
• Students assist with hosting duties when requested, including greeting speakers and
facilitating Q and A.
Journal clubs and group meetings
• Participation in a journal club is strongly encouraged each term to build literature
mastery and critical analysis.
70
• Labs may run group meetings where students present updates, troubleshoot methods,
and practice talks; active participation is expected.
Internal symposia and research days
• The Department or College may host research symposia. Students are expected to
submit abstracts and present posters or talks when feasible.
• Advisors and the GPC may use these venues for formative feedback and milestone
readiness checks.
12.4 Career development and professional preparation
Career philosophy
Graduate education prepares scientists for impactful careers across academia, industry,
government, non-profit, and entrepreneurship. The Department values diverse career pathways
and supports students in exploring and preparing for their chosen trajectories.
Individual Development Plan (IDP)
• Students create an IDP in the first semester and update it annually. The IDP outlines
research, skill-building, and career goals for the next 12 months and 3 years.
• Discuss the IDP with the advisor during annual review; PhD students may also share
highlights with the committee after candidacy.
• Use the IDP to plan conference presentations, manuscripts, internships, certifications,
and teaching experiences.
Core professional competencies
Students should demonstrate growth in the following:
• Scientific communication: clear writing, compelling figures, and effective oral presen-
tations for specialist and general audiences.
• Project management: scoping aims, estimating timelines, tracking risks, and delivering
milestones.
• Collaboration and leadership: teamwork across disciplines; mentoring undergradu-
ates; constructive peer feedback.
• Quantitative fluency: experimental design, statistics, and computational literacy
relevant to the thesis or dissertation.
• Ethics and compliance: responsible authorship, data stewardship, and safety practices.
Conferences and travel
• Presenting at scientific meetings is strongly encouraged. Discuss venue selection, author-
ship order, and timelines with the advisor.
71
• Pre-approval: submit a travel request to the Department at least 4 weeks before the
event with title, abstract, budget, funding sources, and justification. External travel
support may be available from advisors’ grants, the Department, College, or University.
• Students are responsible for following University travel policies and sponsor rules; retain
receipts and submit reports as required.
Internships and experiential learning
• Internships or short-term external research experiences may be permitted with advisor
and GPC approval if they do not delay degree progress and align with the IDP.
• For funded students, any outside engagement must comply with sponsor and employment
policies and be approved in writing.
Professional documents and profiles
• Maintain a current CV and, when appropriate, a resume tailored to non-academic roles.
• Create and maintain an ORCID and professional profiles consistent with advisor guidance
and sponsor expectations.
• Build a simple portfolio of abstracts, preprints, posters, talks, and open datasets or code
when permitted.
Job search support
• Use University career services for workshops on resumes, interviewing, and offer negotia-
tion. Seek field-specific mentoring from the advisor and committee.
• Typical timelines: academia 6 to 12 months lead time; industry 2 to 4 months;
government 3 to 9 months depending on clearance; adjust for publication and defense
schedules.
• Conduct mock talks and interviews with peers and mentors; request feedback on research
statements and teaching philosophies.
12.5 Mentoring, outreach, and community impact
Mentoring undergraduates
• Graduate students are encouraged to mentor undergraduates in research, especially from

• Establish written expectations, provide constructive feedback, and model rigorous, ethical
research conduct.
Outreach and engagement
• As part of DSU’s HBCU mission, students are encouraged to engage in outreach such as

12.7 Checklists
TA onboarding
• Pedagogy orientation and course-specific training completed.

Chapter 13
Administrative Timelines, Leaves,
Forms, and Transfers
13.1 Purpose
This chapter consolidates administrative policies and procedures that govern progress to
degree, continuous enrollment, leaves of absence, transfer of credit, sustaining status, and
required forms. It also provides checklists and timelines to prevent avoidable delays. University
and SGAES policies are authoritative; where there is any conflict, University policy prevails.
13.2 Normative timelines and maximum time to degree
Normative timelines
• MS programs: designed for completion in approximately 2 years of full-time study,
including summers.
• PhD in Neuroscience: typically 4 to 6 years depending on research complexity, publication
goals, and committee expectations.
Upper limits and reviews
University policy sets maximum time limits for degree completion. Students approaching
the maximum must consult the advisor and GPC to file an extension request if permitted
by University rules. The Department may require a written completion plan with specific
deliverables and dates.
75
13.3 Registration, continuous enrollment, and sustain-
ing status
Continuous enrollment
Graduate students must be registered each fall and spring until the degree is conferred.
Acceptable registrations include coursework, thesis or dissertation credits, or sustaining status
after completing required credits. Summer registration is required if the student will use
University resources substantially (for example, defend or submit in summer) per Graduate
School guidance.
Sustaining thesis or dissertation status
After completing required coursework and minimum research credits, students register for
sustaining status to remain active while completing research and writing. Students in
sustaining status must maintain regular engagement with the advisor and, for PhD, hold
annual committee meetings after candidacy. Funding while in sustaining status is not
guaranteed and depends on assistantship availability and satisfactory progress.
Credit load and assistantships
Students holding assistantships must meet Graduate School full-time registration requirements.
Deviations require prior written approval from the advisor, GPC, and Department Chair.
13.4 Leaves, withdrawals, and readmission
Leave of absence
Students who need to interrupt their studies should request a formal leave of absence. A
typical request includes a brief rationale, expected start and return terms, funding implications,
and advisor concurrence. Approved leaves pause academic timelines; students may lose access
to some services while on leave. Compliance approvals (for example, IACUC, IRB, IBC) may
require reactivation and retraining upon return.
Medical or parental leave
Medical or parental needs may qualify for specific accommodations under University policy.
Students should consult the Graduate School and University offices to coordinate documen-
tation, benefits, and return-to-study plans. The Department will work with students and
advisors to plan a safe and timely transition back to research.
Voluntary withdrawal
A student intending to withdraw from the program should notify the advisor, GPC Chair, and
Department Chair in writing and follow University procedures. Students should coordinate
76
data, materials, and authorship matters with the advisor before departure.
Readmission
Former students seeking to return must apply for readmission through the Graduate School
and may be required to meet any updated program requirements. The Department will assess
prior progress, research feasibility, and mentor availability.
13.5 Early completion and acceleration
MS
Students may accelerate timelines with advisor and GPC approval if research and coursework
are completed to program standards.
PhD
Requests for early completion (for example, finishing in 4 years) require evidence of exceptional
research productivity and readiness, typically including multiple first-authored manuscripts
or approved equivalents, along with approvals from the dissertation committee, GPC, and
Department Chair.
13.6 Transfer of graduate credits
Eligibility
Up to 9 graduate credits earned with grades of B or higher at accredited institutions may
be applied to the MS or PhD with approval from the advisor, GPC, and Graduate School.
Courses must closely match DSU curriculum and align with the approved plan of study.
Documentation
An official transcript and, when requested, a syllabus are required for evaluation. Transfers
are recorded after matriculation and approval; limit and age of credits follow University
policy.
13.7 Outside employment and effort commitments
Students supported by DSU funds or DSU-administered grants must obtain prior written
permission from the advisor, GPC, and Department Chair before accepting outside employ-
ment. Any approved outside activity must not conflict with academic progress, research
responsibilities, or sponsor rules.

13.8 Advising changes and program transfers
Changing advisors
Students may request an advisor change for academic or professional reasons. The GPC
facilitates the transition subject to mentor availability and funding. A change requires written
acknowledgment from the new advisor, notification to the current advisor, and updates to
committee membership and Graduate School records. Data, materials, and IP transitions
must follow University and sponsor policies.
Changing programs within the Department
Students wishing to change degree programs (for example, MS to PhD or between MS
programs) must submit a new application or petition per Graduate School procedures.
Admission to a new program is competitive and depends on faculty support and capacity.
Prior credits may be applied as permitted by policy.
13.9 Graduation term planning and deadlines
Graduation planning
At least one term before the intended graduation:
• Confirm all degree requirements with the advisor and, where applicable, the committee.
• Review Graduate School deadlines for formatting checks, defense scheduling, and final
submission for the target term.
• Apply for graduation per Graduate School instructions.
Defense term checklist
• Schedule public seminar and defense; announce per Department norms.
• Provide a complete draft to the committee at least 2 weeks before the defense (3 if
required by University policy).
• Verify compliance approvals and training are current; finalize data archival and authorship
plans.
• After defense, complete revisions, secure signatures, and submit the final document and
forms by Graduate School deadlines.

13.11 Records, data, and compliance continuity
Research records
Students must maintain complete, accessible research records (lab notebooks, raw data,
processed data, analysis code) throughout enrollment. Before any leave, withdrawal, or
graduation, coordinate with the advisor to archive and transfer records per policy.
Compliance renewals
Long leaves or program pauses may require retraining and reactivation of approvals (for
example, IACUC, IRB, IBC) before research resumes. Plan renewals to avoid delays.
